introduction.text: Castello di Giulio II is a late‑15th‑century defensive complex located at the southern edge of Ostia Antica in Rome. It exemplifies the transition from medieval to modern fortification design and played a key role in protecting Rome’s coast and securing supply routes during the Renaissance.

history.description: Between 1423 and 1424 Pope Martin V erected a circular tower with a surrounding moat to guard the river area near the saltworks and to serve as a papal customs post.
Cardinal Guillaume d’Estouteville reinforced the walls of the village, expanding its fortifications between 1461 and 1483.
Construction of the main castle began in 1483 at the behest of Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, future Pope Julius II, to strengthen Rome’s coastal defense and secure food supplies.
In 1556 the castle suffered severe damage during an assault by the Duke of Alba, Fernando Álvarez de Toledo.
The castle was abandoned in 1557 after a catastrophic flood altered the course of the Tiber and turned the surrounding area into unhealthy swamps.

design.description: The fort has a triangular layout with three towers—two circular and one polygonal—connected by a single rampart. It was originally surrounded by a moat fed by the Tiber. The walls are built of thick brick, angled to deflect artillery fire, and feature gun embrasures called troniere.

art.description: The monumental staircase of the castle is decorated with a fresco by Baldassarre Peruzzi depicting mythological scenes related to Hercules.
